title: An 8% Learned Energy Saving That Was a Plant-Model Artefact: Processor-in-the-Loop Evaluation of Rule-Based and Learned Electric-Vehicle Energy Management on a Microcontroller
running_head: M. Gonugondla et al.: An 8% Learned Energy Saving That Was a Plant-Model Artefact

abstract: Learned energy managers for electric vehicles are mostly evaluated in simulation, with the vehicle model taken on trust. In a processor-in-the-loop study, a Soft Actor-Critic policy running on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller at 100 Hz appeared to use 8.28% less energy than a rule-based manager. The gain came from the vehicle model, which billed battery power at the policy's chosen ceiling but computed acceleration from the uncapped torque; a sweep with no controller in the loop reproduced it. The validation gate on logged trips never exercised that path. Anomalies in the campaign tables, not the gates, triggered the audit, and three checks that would have caught it earlier are given. After the correction the learned policy used more energy than the rules in 11 of 12 distinct conditions on the target, by a median of 0.31% (95% interval 0.17% to 0.76%). A dynamic-programming bound explains the null result: with speed fixed by the tracking loop, the rules sit within 0.16% of the optimum. The measured gain lay in the speed loop instead. A two-state Kalman speed estimator cut the energy lost at ten times the sensor-noise floor from 9.44 to 0.24 Wh/km on the target, and learned fault reviewers that classified better offline controlled worse in the loop in simulation. A Transformer power forecaster ran in 36.46 ms of a 40 ms budget, 64% above its estimate. Every result is labelled as measured on the target or simulated on the host, and missed acceptance criteria are reported as misses.
index_terms: Electric vehicles, energy management, Kalman filters, microcontrollers, processor-in-the-loop, reinforcement learning, simulation artefacts, vehicle modelling.
